rationale: B wins because it turns the question a reporter will actually chase into a full angle: "Can a payroll vendor's AI tell you to reclassify a worker — and who's liable when it's wrong?" A is cleaner and more disciplined, but it buries that same issue as proof and refuses the litigation frame with "Deel launches AI compliance tool amid espionage lawsuit with rival" as off-beat, which is too tidy for a company already in a high-profile fight. B still needs tightening because "real-time classification risk engine" is not in the supplied facts, but its story map is sharper.
gaps_in_A: "deciding whether your contractor is legally an employee" overstates the product. The update says the tool flags risks and checks exposure, not that it decides classification.

"Deel launches AI compliance tool amid espionage lawsuit with rival" is refused too defensively. The lawsuit is likely reporter bait; pretending it is only a crisis-holding issue leaves the founder underprepared.
The liability question is strong enough to be its own angle, but A keeps "who bears liability" mostly in proof requirements and uncomfortable questions.
"tracks all 150 in real time" decorates the facts. The update says the tool checks across 150 countries as a company hires; it does not disclose real-time legal updating.
gaps_in_B: "turning that into a real-time classification risk engine" invents mechanics. The update does not say Deel uses payroll/compliance data to power the tool or that it operates in real time.
"tell you to reclassify a worker" overstates the supplied facts. The tool flags risks; it is not described as issuing reclassification instructions.
"positioning itself as the trustworthy compliance arbiter" is a sharp frame, but it needs outside support. Otherwise the lawsuit angle can slide from strategy into insinuation.
"pressures rivals who'd charge for the same capability" is an inference without named competitor pricing. B flags the proof need, but the angle still leans on it.
